blocks.text: A couple trying for a baby learn that the man's testes make two quite different products, a hormone and a gamete, and that each depends on a different pituitary signal. Why can a testis fail to make sperm while still making testosterone, or the reverse? The answer lies in two cell types and a pair of feedback loops.

blocks.markdown:
**Structure and the two functions of the testis.** The testis has two compartments that carry out two functions:

- The **interstitium** contains **Leydig cells**, which synthesise **testosterone** from cholesterol.
- The **seminiferous tubules** contain **Sertoli cells** and developing germ cells and are where **spermatogenesis** takes place.

The testes lie in the scrotum, where the temperature is about 2-3 degrees Celsius below core temperature, which is required for normal spermatogenesis; undescended testes (cryptorchidism) are at higher temperature and the germ cells are damaged.

blocks.title: Hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular axis
blocks.text: GnRH from the hypothalamus is released in pulses (about every 90-120 minutes) and stimulates the anterior pituitary gonadotrophs to release LH and FSH. LH acts on Leydig cells to produce testosterone; FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis and to secrete inhibin B. Testosterone and inhibin feed back negatively on the hypothalamus and pituitary.

blocks.markdown:
**Roles of LH and FSH.**

- **LH** binds receptors on **Leydig cells** and stimulates conversion of cholesterol to **testosterone**, which is secreted into blood and into the seminiferous tubules.
- **FSH** binds receptors on **Sertoli cells**. Sertoli cells (the 'nurse cells') nourish and support germ cells, form the **blood-testis barrier** by tight junctions (creating an immunologically protected compartment for developing sperm), secrete androgen-binding protein (keeping testosterone concentrated in the tubule), secrete fluid, and secrete **inhibin B**.
- **Testosterone** acts through the Sertoli cell (germ cells lack androgen receptors) and, together with FSH, is required to maintain spermatogenesis. Intratesticular testosterone concentrations are many times higher than those in plasma.

**Actions of testosterone** include male sexual differentiation in the fetus, development of male secondary sexual characteristics at puberty, anabolic effects on muscle and bone, libido and stimulation of erythropoiesis. In some tissues it is converted to **dihydrotestosterone (DHT)** by 5-alpha-reductase (prostate, external genitalia, hair follicles) or to oestradiol by aromatase.

**Negative feedback.** The male axis has two feedback loops.

- **Testosterone** inhibits GnRH release from the hypothalamus and LH release from the pituitary, which holds testosterone within its range.
- **Inhibin B**, produced by Sertoli cells, selectively inhibits **FSH** secretion by the pituitary, linking FSH levels to the state of spermatogenesis.

This arrangement explains clinical patterns. Failure of the testes themselves (**primary hypogonadism**, for example after mumps orchitis or in Klinefelter syndrome) lowers testosterone and inhibin, so LH and FSH **rise**. Failure of the pituitary or hypothalamus (**secondary hypogonadism**) gives low testosterone with **low or inappropriately normal** LH and FSH. Exogenous testosterone (or anabolic steroids) inhibits GnRH and LH, so Leydig cell stimulation and intratesticular testosterone fall, sperm production falls and the testes shrink, even though serum testosterone is high.

rows: Loss of negative feedback from the testis
Exogenous testosterone or anabolic steroid use

blocks.markdown:
**Stages of spermatogenesis.** Spermatogenesis proceeds from the periphery of the seminiferous tubule towards the lumen.

1. **Spermatogonia** (diploid, 2n) divide by mitosis, renewing the stem cell pool and producing cells that enter meiosis.
2. **Primary spermatocytes** (2n) undergo **meiosis I**, producing two **secondary spermatocytes** (haploid, n).
3. Each secondary spermatocyte undergoes **meiosis II**, producing two **spermatids** (n). One primary spermatocyte therefore gives **four spermatids**.
4. **Spermiogenesis:** spermatids, without further division, differentiate into **spermatozoa** (acrosome formation, nuclear condensation, flagellum development, loss of most cytoplasm).
5. Sperm are released into the lumen (spermiation) and are carried to the epididymis, where they mature and acquire motility.

The process takes about **70-74 days** in the seminiferous tubule, followed by transit through the epididymis of about 10-14 days, so a sperm in the ejaculate began its development roughly 3 months earlier. This is why changes to sperm quality, from illness, drugs or heat, show up months later.

blocks.caption: Yield of meiosis in the male: four functional gametes per primary spermatocyte, in contrast to one ovum per oocyte.

blocks.title: How many sperm from a number of spermatocytes?
blocks.prompt: Suppose 250 million primary spermatocytes enter meiosis in a day and no cells are lost. How many spermatozoa result?

steps.text: Each primary spermatocyte produces two secondary spermatocytes by meiosis I.
Each secondary spermatocyte produces two spermatids by meiosis II, and each spermatid becomes one spermatozoon.
In practice some cells are lost by apoptosis, so real yields are lower.

blocks.answer: 1000 million (1 x 10^9) spermatozoa, four per primary spermatocyte.

blocks.title: Interpreting a hormone profile
blocks.prompt: A 33-year-old man with infertility has low testosterone, markedly raised LH and FSH, and small, firm testes. Where is the lesion, and why are LH and FSH raised?

steps.text: Low testosterone means the final hormone is deficient.
High LH and FSH show the pituitary is working and is responding to missing feedback: testosterone normally inhibits GnRH and LH, and inhibin B inhibits FSH, and both are low.
Therefore the lesion is in the testis itself (primary testicular failure).

blocks.answer: Primary testicular failure; reduced testosterone and inhibin remove negative feedback so LH and FSH rise.

items: Sertoli cells: FSH-stimulated support of germ cells, blood-testis barrier, androgen-binding protein, inhibin B.
Testosterone inhibits GnRH and LH; inhibin B selectively inhibits FSH.
Spermatogenesis: spermatogonium, primary spermatocyte, secondary spermatocyte, spermatid, spermatozoon; about 70-74 days plus epididymal transit.
Exogenous testosterone suppresses the axis and spermatogenesis.

blocks.title: Two cell types, two signals
blocks.text: Keep the pairs straight: LH acts on Leydig cells and makes testosterone, FSH acts on Sertoli cells and supports spermatogenesis (with testosterone). Inhibin B reports on tubular function to the pituitary, so FSH is raised in selective tubular damage while LH and testosterone stay near normal.

blocks.title: High serum testosterone does not guarantee fertility
blocks.text: Intratesticular testosterone, driven by LH, is what supports spermatogenesis. Taking testosterone by injection can raise serum levels while suppressing LH and so lowering intratesticular testosterone, reducing sperm production.

points: LH stimulates Leydig cells to make testosterone; FSH acts on Sertoli cells, which support spermatogenesis, form the blood-testis barrier and secrete inhibin B.
Testosterone provides negative feedback on GnRH and LH, while inhibin B selectively suppresses FSH.

Spermatogenesis runs from spermatogonium through primary and secondary spermatocytes and spermatids to spermatozoa, yielding four sperm per primary spermatocyte and taking about 70-74 days plus epididymal transit.
Primary testicular failure raises LH and FSH with low testosterone; exogenous androgens lower LH and FSH and suppress sperm production.

questions.stem: Which cells of the testis synthesise testosterone in response to luteinising hormone?

options.text: Leydig cells
Sertoli cells
Spermatogonia
Epididymal principal cells

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Leydig cells in the interstitium make testosterone from cholesterol.
distractorRationale.b: Sertoli cells respond to FSH and support germ cells.
distractorRationale.d: The epididymis is a duct for sperm maturation.

questions.explanation: LH binds receptors on Leydig cells in the interstitium and stimulates conversion of cholesterol to testosterone. FSH, in contrast, acts on Sertoli cells in the seminiferous tubules.

questions.stem: Which statement about Sertoli cells is correct?

options.text: They respond to FSH, form the blood-testis barrier and secrete inhibin B
They respond to LH and secrete testosterone
They are haploid germ cells that become spermatozoa
They secrete GnRH into the portal blood

questions.correctOptionText: They respond to FSH, form the blood-testis barrier and secrete inhibin B

distractorRationale.a: Correct: they are the supportive 'nurse' cells of the tubule.
distractorRationale.c: Sertoli cells are somatic support cells, not germ cells.
distractorRationale.d: GnRH is produced by hypothalamic neurons.

questions.explanation: Sertoli cells line the seminiferous tubules, nourish germ cells, form the blood-testis barrier by tight junctions, respond to FSH and testosterone and secrete inhibin B, which feeds back on FSH.

questions.stem: Selective damage to the seminiferous tubules, with intact Leydig cells, is most likely to produce which hormonal pattern?

options.text: Raised FSH with normal LH and testosterone because inhibin B is reduced
Raised LH with low FSH
Low FSH and low LH with raised inhibin
Normal FSH with markedly low testosterone

questions.correctOptionText: Raised FSH with normal LH and testosterone because inhibin B is reduced

distractorRationale.a: Correct: loss of Sertoli cell inhibin B releases FSH, while Leydig cells still make testosterone.
distractorRationale.b: LH would not rise selectively when Leydig cells are intact.
distractorRationale.c: Tubular damage reduces, not raises, inhibin.
distractorRationale.d: Testosterone production is preserved with intact Leydig cells.

questions.explanation: Inhibin B from Sertoli cells selectively inhibits FSH. If tubular function is lost, inhibin B falls and FSH rises, whereas intact Leydig cells keep testosterone and therefore LH near normal.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man using anabolic steroid injections has small testes and a very low sperm count. His serum testosterone is high. Which hormonal finding is expected?

options.text: Low LH and FSH because of negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary
High LH and FSH because of testicular failure
High LH with low FSH
High GnRH with high LH

questions.correctOptionText: Low LH and FSH because of negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary

distractorRationale.a: Correct: exogenous androgen suppresses the axis, leaving the testes unstimulated.
distractorRationale.b: High gonadotrophins would indicate primary testicular failure, not suppression.
distractorRationale.d: Negative feedback reduces GnRH and LH.

questions.explanation: Exogenous testosterone inhibits GnRH and LH (and, through reduced Sertoli stimulation, FSH), so the testes lose gonadotrophin support: intratesticular testosterone falls, spermatogenesis fails and the testes shrink, despite high serum testosterone.

questions.stem: Each primary spermatocyte gives rise to four spermatids after meiosis I and II.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Meiosis I yields two secondary spermatocytes, and meiosis II divides each into two spermatids, giving four spermatids per primary spermatocyte, which then become spermatozoa by spermiogenesis.

questions.stem: Spermatogenesis from spermatogonium to released spermatozoon takes 74 days, and transit through the epididymis takes 12 days. How many days before ejaculation did the spermatogonial division that produced a given sperm begin?
questions.explanation: The sperm were produced over 74 days in the tubule and then spent 12 days in the epididymis, so the total is 74 + 12 = 86 days, roughly three months. A toxic insult or a fever therefore affects semen quality about 2-3 months later.

questions.stem: A man produces 120 million spermatozoa per day. Assuming no cell loss and that each primary spermatocyte yields four spermatozoa, how many million primary spermatocytes must complete meiosis per day?
questions.explanation: Meiosis I and II give four spermatids per primary spermatocyte, so the number of primary spermatocytes is 120 / 4 = 30 million per day. In practice, apoptosis during spermatogenesis means more cells must enter the process.

questions.stem: Describe the roles of LH and FSH in testicular function, naming the target cell of each and the products that result.
markingGuide: LH acts on Leydig cells in the interstitium to stimulate testosterone synthesis from cholesterol
FSH acts on Sertoli cells in the seminiferous tubules
Sertoli cells support and nourish germ cells and form the blood-testis barrier
Sertoli cells secrete androgen-binding protein, fluid and inhibin B
Testosterone (acting through Sertoli cells) together with FSH is required for spermatogenesis
Testosterone also drives male secondary sexual characteristics, anabolic effects and libido
questions.explanation: The testis has two compartments with different pituitary controls. Knowing which cell responds to which hormone allows the effect of hypogonadism, or of exogenous hormones, to be predicted.

questions.stem: Explain the negative feedback control of the male reproductive axis by testosterone and inhibin, and predict the LH, FSH and testosterone changes in primary testicular failure and in a man taking exogenous testosterone.
markingGuide: GnRH pulses stimulate pituitary LH and FSH release
Testosterone inhibits GnRH from the hypothalamus and LH from the pituitary
Inhibin B from Sertoli cells selectively inhibits FSH
Primary testicular failure: low testosterone and inhibin, so LH and FSH are high (loss of feedback)
Exogenous testosterone: serum testosterone high, LH and FSH low because of feedback suppression
Consequence of suppression: reduced intratesticular testosterone, impaired spermatogenesis and testicular atrophy
questions.explanation: Feedback explains why gonadotrophins move in the opposite direction to gonadal hormones. It also explains why testosterone therapy can impair fertility.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man has bilateral undescended testes that were never corrected, and semen analysis shows a very low sperm count. Which explanation best fits the effect on spermatogenesis?

options.text: The higher temperature of the abdomen compared with the scrotum damages developing germ cells
Leydig cells cannot respond to LH at body temperature
The blood-testis barrier is absent in the abdomen
Meiosis requires a temperature above core body temperature

questions.correctOptionText: The higher temperature of the abdomen compared with the scrotum damages developing germ cells

distractorRationale.a: Correct: spermatogenesis needs a temperature about 2-3 degrees Celsius below core.
distractorRationale.b: Leydig cell function is relatively preserved; the main defect is germ cell damage.
distractorRationale.c: The barrier is formed by Sertoli cells and is not temperature dependent.
distractorRationale.d: Meiosis requires a temperature lower than core body temperature, not higher.

questions.explanation: Spermatogenesis proceeds best at the scrotal temperature, which is about 2-3 degrees Celsius below core temperature. Testes retained in the abdomen are warmer, so spermatogonia and developing germ cells are damaged and sperm output is reduced, while testosterone production is usually better preserved.
